claims.text: Recruitment attracts suitable applicants for a vacancy; selection chooses the most suitable applicant using relevant criteria. Induction introduces the new employee to the business, colleagues, procedures and role. Further training develops the skills and knowledge needed for work. Start by identifying the vacancy and preparing a job description and person or job specification. Advertise through suitable channels, assess applications consistently, shortlist, interview or use relevant work tests, then appoint and introduce the worker. Develop capability and review progress after appointment. Training can be on-the-job in the work setting or off-the-job away from normal work tasks. These methods differ in resources and suitability; attracting an applicant is not the same as developing a current employee.

claims.text: On-the-job training develops skills while working with guidance from an experienced colleague or supervisor. It can use the actual equipment and avoid travel, but takes the trainer’s time and may pass on poor habits or expose real work to mistakes. Off-the-job training takes place away from normal duties, for example through a course or simulated practice. It can provide specialist teaching and space to learn without disrupting real orders, but costs time and fees and may not match local equipment perfectly. Choose according to the task, safety, existing expertise, cost, time and learning needs. Induction introduces the new worker but does not replace all specialist skill development.

claims.text: Fictional Tano Stores has a patient experienced clerk and a safe practice account on its familiar booking system. A new assistant needs routine booking skills. On-the-job guidance using the practice account suits the local routine and available expertise. An external course could offer broader knowledge but adds cost and may teach a different system. Prefer supervised workplace learning here, checking competence before live work; a specialist or hazardous task without a competent trainer would change the choice.

claims.text: Recruitment documents should describe the same vacancy consistently. A job description states the role’s duties and responsibilities; a job specification states the relevant abilities, qualifications or experience required from the person. An application form gathers comparable evidence against those criteria. An advertisement attracts suitable applicants by stating the role, location, key requirements and how and when to apply. Avoid vague requests for a wonderful person or irrelevant conditions that do not help perform the job. Distinguish essential criteria from desirable experience so useful applicants are not excluded by an unnecessarily high barrier. The documents should support a fair evidence-based comparison, not guarantee that the selected person will perform perfectly.

claims.text: Recruitment identifies a vacancy and attracts a pool of suitable applicants. Define the duties and relevant person criteria before selecting a channel such as an internal notice or external advertisement. Internal recruitment can use known staff and offer progression but restrict the pool; external recruitment can bring new skills but requires assessment and introduction. The aim at this stage is suitable applications, not yet a final appointment.

claims.text: Induction training is an introduction given to a new employee, explaining the firm’s organisational structure, activities and procedures. It can include colleagues, reporting, safety arrangements, role expectations and where to ask for help. It can reduce uncertainty and avoidable early mistakes. It is not a substitute for learning every specialist task. On-the-job and off-the-job methods can support later skill development according to need.

claims.text: Training develops the knowledge and skills required for work. Production or service improvements depend on applying the learning with adequate equipment and support.
